rationale: In ODE screens of curated pathway models, a majority of habituating networks lost habituation when a third node was driven, which is a credible in-silico result. The further suggestion that those nodes would break pharmacoresistance in real tissues is untested.

Sensitization under a 1.5-fold criterion in most curated pathway models, and its rarity in the matched random circuits, matches the reported screen. The comparison leaves open whether that rarity is biological or an artifact of the random-model class.

The same modeling framework reports that third-node stimulation broke sensitization in only a small minority of models and of node pairs. That asymmetry with habituation is plausible inside these ODEs, though it does not dictate which therapies will work.

If random graphs matched on size, degree and the listed centrality scores still lack the memory the biological models show, those particular statistics are not sufficient. Unmeasured features such as motifs or signed kinetics could still be what carries the memory.

Noise can interact with oscillators, but the claim is an explicit hypothesis, and the same study already notes oscillatory models that did not gain memory from noise. Harmonic resonance is a weak analogy for biochemical memory, so a general benefit is not established.

Biological pathway models being more robust to edge rewiring than random graphs fits broader results on evolved-network robustness. Attributing the gap to selection for changing environments is a plausible but untested explanation.

Pulsatile transcription-factor, calcium and kinase signaling is well documented in cells. That cells exploit those pulses as mutual training signals to evolve complex phenotypes is a conjecture, and the claim itself marks the evolutionary role as unknown.

Development, not a direct genetic blueprint, produces the phenotype that selection evaluates, and context-dependent cell behavior is basic experimental embryology. Calling physiology a control layer is a framing, but the separation of genome from selected capacities is secure.

Asexual Schmidtea are mixoploid, with cell-to-cell chromosome-number variation, and fragments above a size threshold regenerate a normal worm with unusual reliability. Very small pieces fail, so 'every fragment' overstates a process that is highly reliable rather than exceptionless.

Many cell-physiological abilities are ancient and were present in unicellular ancestors, unlike nervous systems, which are costly later inventions. Morphogenetic competencies of metazoan cells were also extensively rebuilt during multicellularity, so they do not simply arrive free.

Inside this bubble-sort embryogeny model, more pre-evaluation sorting should reach a monotonic target faster, and the reported generation counts are the kind of outcome that setup produces. The figures are specific to the simulation.

Once cells can repair order before fitness is scored, phenotypic fitness decouples from the structural genes and selection on those genes weakens. A lower genotypic-fitness plateau and wider variance at higher competency is the expected pattern under this fitness definition.

A competent minority that converts poor genomes into fit phenotypes should invade, with the competency needed falling as its starting frequency rises. The exact cutoffs, including failure at 2.5 percent, are simulation details treated as likely reported rather than independently re-derived.

With no cost, an evolvable competency allele can drift once phenotypic fitness is saturated, so a plateau above the minimum needed for maximum fitness is expected. The specific plateau near 470 is a reported run outcome.

If high competency makes the phenotype fit regardless of gene order, the correlation between genotypic and phenotypic fitness must collapse, and an early drop toward zero follows. That this blocks selection on structural genes is true inside the model by how fitness is defined.

Penalizing competency recreates the standard Baldwin pattern: early physiological compensation, later improvement of structural genes, and a decline in the costly trait. Real developmental-competency costs remain unmeasured, but the in-silico result is coherent.

Asexual planarians do combine a chaotic, mixoploid genome with very stable anatomy. Explaining that pair by runaway competency that blocked selection on structural genes is untested; asexuality and weak purifying selection already account for much of the genomic disorder.

Stable Mendelian morphological mutant strains, routine in flies and mice, have not been established in planarians, and a permanently two-headed line from a bioelectric or gap-junction perturbation is a real reported line. RNA interference yields many morphological phenotypes, so 'the only abnormal line' is too absolute.

In a model with one evolvable competency locus and fifty structural loci, more recorded changes at the competency locus is a bookkeeping outcome of that run. It describes the simulation's genetics, not a measurement on real genomes.

Hiding genetic defects from selection can, in a toy model, favor further competency. A general ratchet that locks evolution into improving the intelligence of cellular material is an extrapolation far beyond a one-dimensional sorting embryo.

Adaptive physiology and developmental plasticity long predate brains and do bias evolutionary paths. Treating problem-solving intelligence as a distinct driver of pre-neural evolution goes beyond the accepted roles of plasticity and developmental bias.

Evolving neural cellular automata so that local metabolic rewards yield a body-wide French-flag pattern is a reported result of this evolutionary search. It shows the model can scale a cell-level reward into a tissue pattern, not that embryos evolved by that route.

An attractor learned from a uniform start often reconstructs poorly from random initial conditions, so that half fits the model. Real embryos are not a homogeneous baseline; maternal polarity and localized determinants are widespread, so the biological analogy fails.

A pattern that is an attractor of the selected dynamics will often be restored after small later perturbations and lost after very large ones. Repair without an explicit repair reward is expected for this kind of system and is credibly what the runs showed.

A stress variable that spikes immediately before a spontaneous remodeling wave is a specific simulation observation. Precedence in one model does not show that stress causes the change rather than covarying with it.

If the French-flag pattern is a stable attractor, persistence from the selected horizon out to a thousand steps needs no extra fitness term. That conclusion is fair for this model and does not transfer automatically to real adult tissues.

Clamping stress to zero in a tissue that uses it, and thereby losing pattern accuracy and the red stripe, is a concrete in-silico intervention, including the reported percentages. The claim correctly limits itself to that stress-using tissue.

A very high imposed stress that leaves cell states unchanged at once but changes them later fits a delayed or threshold response. It does not establish that stress was encoded to be instructive only at specific concentrations.

Most of ten evolved tissues still patterning after stress is removed supports dispensability for the basic French flag. One stress-using tissue scoring better after a mid-course target change, at a marginal p-value, is only weak evidence that stress improves adaptation.

Larger transfer entropy from a cell's stress into its neighbors than into itself would favor a paracrine reading and is a measurable outcome on this lattice. On a small evolved system that statistic is easy to over-read as the unique signaling mode.

A reversal over time in which stripe's state predicts the other is a possible information-flow pattern in the simulation. Calling the leading region an organizer that takes turns imports an embryological concept the entropy reversal does not demonstrate.

The order of transfer-entropy peaks between energy and cell state can be measured, but peak order does not show that an anatomical loop first controls the energy cells need. The top-down conclusion is an interpretation of a correlational statistic.

Stress rising as local active information falls is a joint statistic the model can produce, and it lines up with stressors as unpredictable events. That alignment does not show that evolution used stress as a channel switched on by memory failure.

A model that sits in a stable pattern and then abruptly remodels licenses a prediction that some finished-looking phenotypes will still change if watched longer. A single planarian follow-up gives partial support and does not secure the general prediction.

Transient ERK inhibition after amputation leaves many Dugesia fragments headless, and later spontaneous repatterning in a minority of a large cohort is a specific reported outcome. Exact percentages could shift with how repatterning is scored, so the precise fractions stay slightly uncertain.

Restoration weeks after ERK blockade, if it occurred, shows a slow tissue dynamic in that experiment. Planarian remodeling, degrowth and rescaling were already known to run for weeks to months, so a timescale 'much longer than previously known' overclaims novelty.

A transient move away from the target while misplaced cells are cleared is ordinary attractor dynamics and can look like delayed gratification. That this was not an explicit fitness term is fair; the cognitive 'free lunch' wording is stronger than the simulation requires.

The animals were amputated and held headless with an ERK inhibitor, so later change is not regeneration in a body that was never injured. The result does not show that a missing-tissue response is unnecessary for normal regeneration.

Bacterial biofilms use metabolic and potassium-stress oscillations, and somitogenesis uses a clock and a wavefront, but that wavefront is not a generic stress code. A conserved stress mechanism scaling patterning from bacteria through animals to this simulation is a speculative unification.

Metazoan cells retain ancient sensing, signaling and physiological control that were co-opted for development. They also narrowed or lost many free-living behaviors as they differentiated, so an undiminished cognitive repertoire simply scaled to anatomy is too strong.

Ion channels, transmitters and gap junctions function both in morphogenesis and in behavior, so molecular continuity is real. That evolution pivoted morphogenetic collective intelligence into behavioral intelligence by scaling homeostatic setpoints is a proposal, not a demonstrated historical transition.

The genotype-to-anatomy map is highly non-invertible, which blocks any simple writing of a desired anatomy back into the genes. Weismann's barrier remains a major limit in animals, and the routes that sometimes cross it do not generally encode adaptive somatic experience into the germline.

Cells respond adaptively and selection on intercellular signals matters, but a large share of documented anatomical evolution is change in local cis-regulatory and protein interactions. The claim that evolution mainly searches behavior-shaping signals rather than local rules is not supported.

Indirect developmental encoding compresses phenotype relative to a one-gene-one-trait map and can favor robustness. Equating the genome with a variational autoencoder that inevitably produces general-purpose problem-solvers overstates both the analogy and the outcome, since many lineages evolve narrow specialists.

Gap junctions couple electrical and chemical state across cells and are required for several developmental and regenerative patterns, which enlarges the spatial scale of coordination. They do not erase cell individuality; cells keep distinct identities and gene-expression states.

Dissociated Xenopus embryonic ectoderm self-organizes into motile ciliated spheroids with behaviors absent from intact epidermis, the published Xenobot result. Dissociation and culture conditions contribute along with release from neighbor signals, but the phenomenon is solid.

Bacillus biofilms propagate potassium waves that coordinate metabolism, so bacterial electrical signaling is real and ancient. Osmoregulation and metabolism are the clearer early uses; that biofilms adopted ion-channel networks for the same computational reason as brains is a narrative overlay.

Bioelectric prepatterns regionalize the vertebrate face, and changing voltage with ion channels can induce ectopic eye tissue in Xenopus outside the usual competence field for Pax6. Locating those eyes specifically on the gut or tail mixes channel-misexpression results with separate surgical tail-eye grafts.

Xenopus tadpoles whose native eyes are suppressed and that carry a grafted tail eye can use that eye for light-cued learning, including cases where axons enter the spinal cord. Not every graft succeeds, but animals can see this way without multi-generation adaptation.

In highly polyploid newt larvae, pronephric tubules that are multicellular in diploids are built by fewer, larger cells, and at extreme ploidy one cell forms the lumen by wrapping around itself. Preserving the organ while changing cell number is a classic result; downward causation is a gloss on that fact.

An intermediate physiological layer can in principle split a hard control problem, and some voltage patterns track anatomy more directly than any single channel gene. It has not been shown that both the gene-to-voltage map and the voltage-to-anatomy map are actually easier to invert than the direct map.

Tadpole tail regeneration depends on a V-ATPase-driven hyperpolarized state, and a yeast proton pump with no meaningful sequence homology can restore that voltage and rescue regeneration. That is direct evidence that the instructive variable is the bioelectric state rather than the identity of the pump.

A brief gap-junction or ion-channel perturbation can reset wild-type Dugesia so fragments regenerate two heads and keep doing so. Persistent altered signaling or tissue polarity can store that state; a freely replaceable target-morphology memory is a slightly stronger reading than the perturbations alone require.

Gap-junction blockade during regeneration of Girardia dorotocephala was reported to produce head shapes resembling other planarian species. The resemblance is qualitative and overlaps generic proportioning defects, so crossing 100–150 million years of morphospace overstates the anatomical result.

Surgical rotation of a patch of Paramecium cortex is inherited through many fissions, and the reversed ciliary rows continue to beat so that food is pushed the wrong way despite a wild-type genome. Cortical inheritance in ciliates is a standard, well-replicated exception to DNA-only structural heredity.

Planarians exposed to barium, a potassium-channel blocker, can lose anterior tissue and later regenerate heads that tolerate barium, which is acute physiological adaptation. A change in only a handful of genes is a strong quantitative claim and is easy to overstate relative to a typical transcriptome response.

Highly regenerative animals such as planarians and salamanders are not especially cancer-prone, and asexual planarians show little obvious senescence, against a simple stem-cell theory of cancer risk. Regeneration, cancer suppression and aging resistance do not travel together as a general rule across animals.

A feedback loop in which competency weakens selection on structural genes appears in the authors' simulations. That this ratchet has run to different degrees in planarians, salamanders and mammals lacks independent phylogenetic or genetic evidence.

Planarians lack the morphological mutant collections of flies and mice, germline transgenesis has been unusually difficult, and permanent two-head lines have come from physiological edits. Mixoploidy and asexual reproduction explain those facts without a competency ratchet, so the model does not earn the explanation.

Developmental buffering can shrink phenotypic differences among genotypes and allow mutations that a brittle map would eliminate, which is a standard evolvability argument. Robustness can also hide variation from selection, so more efficient search and escape from local maxima are not guaranteed.

Canalization and chaperone capacitance hide genetic differences that stay phenotypically silent until stress or a new background reveals them. That regulative development accumulates cryptic variation is mainstream evolutionary genetics.

Physarum habituates to repeated aversive stimuli and solves foraging problems as one syncytium, and its behavior is change of body shape. Directed growth toward the heavier of distant inert objects is a narrower and less settled report than habituation itself.

A modern planarian study found savings: animals regenerated from trained tails relearned a task faster, which is weaker than recall of the original memory. Mid-century claims that regenerated worms fully retained trained information were not reliably replicated.

Xenopus tadpoles with no primary eyes and one eye on the tail can perform visual learning through that eye, which can innervate the spinal cord. Success depends on the graft, but the within-generation adaptation of existing cellular hardware is a published result.

Channel gating is post-translational, and membrane voltage depends on open probabilities, pumps and ionic history, so different channel sets can share a voltage map and one set can sit at different voltages. Transcript or protein levels therefore cannot replace measurements in living tissue.

Non-neural bioelectric networks coordinate cell behavior toward tissue-scale anatomical outcomes, and that role is not confined to brains. Describing them as cognitive glue that binds cellular goals into a larger cognitive light cone is a theoretical vocabulary rather than an established mechanism.

Ion channels, gap junctions and many transmitters function in development and in non-neural cells and predate nervous systems, which is why neural reagents act elsewhere in the body. Their earliest roles were likely osmotic and metabolic, so a morphogenesis-first origin of neural signaling is only partly supported.

Axolotl limbs are notable for regenerating successfully across repeated amputations. When regeneration eventually declines, cell depletion, scarring or aging are more plausible causes than habituation of a pattern memory that gives up.

Injury to a growing antler can reappear as an extra tine at the same site in later years, after the rack is shed, a long-studied positional memory of the pedicle. The store is the antlerogenic periosteum more specifically than generic scalp cells, but the yearly memory is real.

Transient disruption of planarian gap-junctional or bioelectric signaling yields two-headed regenerates whose fragments keep making two heads across later cuts until an experimental reset. That genome-independent shift in regenerative target is a repeated finding in this system.

The same wild-type planarian cells can regenerate one head, two heads or none after physiological or knockdown perturbations, so head number is not a fixed readout of genotype. The genome still encodes the channels and signals that make those outcomes possible; the software metaphor names that history dependence.

Genetic assimilation is a coherent theoretical possibility, and ion-channel sequence changes can alter voltage phenotypes that matter to anatomy. There is no comparative evidence that assimilating bioelectric states has been an important route in the evolution of body plans.

A characterized planarian commensal, or products associated with it, can push regeneration toward two heads, in the same broad class as microbial effects on host development. How widely commensals do this, as opposed to one reported interaction, is narrower than the wording.

Voltage-reporter patterns in anatomically normal planarians can predict whether a later cut will make one head or two, so the pattern is not merely a readout of current shape. Normal gene expression throughout, and the stronger description as a counterfactual memory of a future body, are less directly shown.

After certain ion-channel or gap-junction treatments, planarian lines regenerate as one-headed or two-headed in an apparently stochastic alternation across successive cuts. That history-dependent bistability is a reported experimental outcome; the likeness to perceptual bistability is optional.
